name: Fever Ray
label: Rabid Records / Mute
lede: Karin Dreijer fronted a Gothenburg guitar band, started The Knife with brother Olof, then stepped out alone in a mask as Fever Ray. In 2023 they made an album about love that Pitchfork ranked No. 8 for the year.

eras.title: Guitars first, then a brother
eras.text: Karin Dreijer fronts Honey Is Cool, a Gothenburg guitar band, until it ends in July 2000. Next comes a synth duo with brother Olof Dreijer, and Rabid Records outlives both.

years.src: Wikipedia: Honey Is Cool · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: Karin Dreijer fronts Honey Is Cool, a Gothenburg guitar band
years.p: Dreijer, born April 7, 1975, picked up guitar at ten. The final line-up adds John Jern, Staffan Larsson, Tina Weibull and Fredrik Wennerlund.
years.xp:
Wikipedia describes Dreijer as the band's frontperson and main creative force from 1994 to 2000, and says they moved to Stockholm in 1998. Honey Is Cool went from Sunspot to MVG and then to a label of their own.

The band's name for that label was Rabid Records. Wikipedia's Honey Is Cool page credits the band with setting it up; its Knife page credits the duo. Either way, Rabid outlived both.

years.h: Honey Is Cool's debut, Crazy Love, comes out on MVG
years.p: A band record of guitars and keyboards, a long way from the pitch-shifted voice that comes later.

years.h: Early Morning Are You Working? is the last Honey Is Cool record
years.p: The band splits a year later. In Gothenburg, [[The Knife|bf710b71-48e5-4e15-9bd6-96debb2e4e98]] is already underway.

years.src: Wikipedia: Honey Is Cool · Wikipedia: The Knife
years.h: Honey Is Cool splits on July 3, and Dreijer moves on
years.p: Wikipedia says Dreijer wanted to focus on a new project, and drummer Fredrik Wennerlund had other plans.
years.xp: The new project was The Knife, formed with Olof Dreijer in Gothenburg in 1999. Wikipedia notes that ideas from Honey Is Cool songs resurface on The Knife's 2003 album Deep Cuts.

eras.title: Two siblings, a label, and an ad nobody planned
eras.text: The Knife's first two albums come out on Rabid, a Grammis goes uncollected, and a Swedish folk singer's cover of one song lands in a TV ad.

years.h: Karin and Olof Dreijer put out The Knife on their own label
years.p: A synth-pop debut on Rabid Records, the company the siblings run together.

years.h: Deep Cuts, later No. 4 on Sonic's list of the best Swedish albums
years.p: Rabid released it January 17, with "Heartbeats" already out as a single. Pitchfork gave it 7.6, and Mute issued it in the US on October 31, 2006.
years.xp: The singles were "Heartbeats" (December 27, 2002), "You Take My Breath Away" (March 28, 2003) and "Pass This On" (June 13, 2005), per Wikipedia. The Sonic ranking is its list of the 100 best Swedish albums ever.

years.h: The Knife win a Grammis and send the Guerrilla Girls to collect it
years.p: After winning Pop Group of the Year, the duo boycotted the Swedish ceremony. Two Guerrilla Girls representatives went instead, in costumes marked with the number 50.
years.xp: The protest was aimed at male dominance in the music industry, per Wikipedia. The Knife skipped later Grammis ceremonies too, sometimes sending manipulated videos, and kept to beaked Venetian-style masks in promo photos.

years.h: José González covers "Heartbeats" and a Sony ad does the rest
years.p: The Bravia commercial used González's acoustic version, which Wikipedia says did better than The Knife's original and reached No. 9 in the UK.
years.xp: According to Wikipedia, the duo defended taking the money by saying they needed it to start a record company, Rabid, despite their anti-commercial stance. Wikipedia's two pages disagree on whether the ad ran in 2005 or 2006; the song page says November 2005.

eras.title: Masks on, lights out
eras.text: With Silent Shout the siblings go from a studio project to a stage act, and Dreijer's solo work starts in earnest.

years.h: Silent Shout goes to No. 1 in Sweden
years.p: Recorded in Stockholm between March 2004 and November 2005. Wikipedia says Pitchfork named it the best album of 2006.
years.xp: Karin Dreijer's pitch-shifted, multi-tracked vocals are what the record is known for. The singles were "Silent Shout," "Marble House," "We Share Our Mothers' Health" and "Like a Pen." Pitchfork later ranked the title track at No. 74 on its list of the 2000s' top tracks and the album 15th among the decade's best.

years.cap: Olof Dreijer on stage with The Knife, 2006
years.h: After seven years in the studio, The Knife play live
years.p: Wikipedia says the duo's first live performances came only in 2006, and that the shows sold out worldwide.

years.src: Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer · Wikipedia: The Knife
years.h: Dreijer's solo debut song becomes the Vikings theme
years.p: "If I Had a Heart" came out in 2008 under the name Fever Ray, and later turned up in Breaking Bad and Horns.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists appearances in Person of Interest, Breaking Bad, Wentworth and Laurence Anyways as well. Dreijer had also guested with [[Röyksopp|1c70a3fc-fa3c-4be1-8b55-c3192db8a884]] on "What Else Is There?" in 2005 and on their Junior tracks in 2009.

eras.title: Two projects at once
eras.text: Dreijer releases a solo album as Fever Ray while The Knife, with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock, works on an opera about Darwin.

years.src: Wikipedia: Fever Ray (2009 album) · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: Under a new name, Dreijer releases a solo album on Rabid
years.p: Digital release January 12, physical on March 18. Pitchfork gave it 8.1 and placed it 9th on its 2009 year-end list.
years.xp: Wikipedia says The Guardian named it the second-best album of 2009, and The Observer called it "an astonishingly stark record." AllMusic compared its isolation to Björk's Homogenic. Singles: "If I Had a Heart," "When I Grow Up," "Triangle Walks" and "Seven."

years.h: Coachella gets Fever Ray in a mask and body paint
years.p: Wikipedia says the 2010 set drew positive reviews. Dreijer played in costume behind gauze screens.
years.xp: The Electric Picnic set in Ireland followed that September. Wikipedia describes the live look as theatrical costumes, masks and body paint, with gauze screens in front.

years.h: The Knife write an opera about Darwin with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock
years.p: The score is for Hotel Pro Forma's stage piece on On the Origin of Species. Pitchfork gave the 92-minute album 6.9.
years.xp: Wikipedia says it was recorded in Berlin, Stockholm and Copenhagen during 2008-2009 and marks Darwin's 150th anniversary. Drowned in Sound gave it 10/10; BBC Music called it "complicated, esoteric and, yes, really quite bonkers." Wikipedia's page gives February 1 as the release date while The Knife's page says March 1, so it is dated to the year here.

years.h: Dreijer scores a Bergman play at Stockholm's Royal Dramatic Theatre
years.p: Hour of the Wolf, adapted from Ingmar Bergman, premiered March 12, 2011. Dreijer scored Vahák in 2016.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists both theatre scores next to the Fever Ray and Knife records, so the stage work runs alongside the albums rather than in the gaps between them.

eras.title: A three-LP argument, then a last show
eras.text: The Knife release a long, political album in 2013, play a final tour the next year and stop.

years.big: "What we do is political. That should be impossible to misunderstand."
years.h: Shaking the Habitual takes its title from Foucault
years.p: The Knife said so in a video interview that April, around the release. Pitchfork's Lindsay Zoladz gave the album 8.4.
years.xp:
Zoladz called it the duo's "most political, ambitious, accomplished album," and added that in a strange way it also feels like their most personal. The Dreijers say it draws on feminist and queer theory, environmentalism and structuralism, and criticizes wealth inequality and the nuclear family. Shannon Funchess of [[Light Asylum|a077a16e-edb1-43b2-99a4-460cab3b6a6e]] sings on "Stay Out Here," with lyrics by artist Emily Roysdon, and Liv Strömquist's comic "End Extreme Wealth" is the artwork.

It reached No. 52 on the Billboard 200 and won the Nordic Music Prize in March 2014, per Wikipedia. The tour opened April 26, 2013 in Bremen. Lead single "Full of Fire" came with a short film by Marit Östberg.

years.cap: The Knife at Terminal 5, New York, May 2014, on the Shaking the Habitual tour
years.h: A last show with a manifesto for a title
years.p: On November 8 at Iceland Airwaves in Reykjavik, the farewell was billed "Post-Colonial Gender Politics Come First, Music Comes Second." It was released as a concert film and a special-edition vinyl set.
years.xp: The duo announced on August 21, 2014 that they were done. Wikipedia says the band ended after the final six dates of the Shaking the Habitual tour, from October 31 to November 8.

eras.title: Plunge, and a fast second act
eras.text: After eight years Fever Ray comes back with a record built by club producers and aimed at the body.

years.cap: Fever Ray at Down The Rabbit Hole festival, on the Plunge tour
years.h: Fever Ray comes back after eight years with Plunge
years.p: "To the Moon and Back" came out October 20, the album October 27. Metacritic scored it 87, and Pitchfork's Philip Sherburne called it "thrillingly restless."
years.xp: Wikipedia lists Paula Temple, Deena Abdelwahed, Nídia, Tami T, [[Peder Mannerfelt|4f9f50e9-7962-4792-86f6-cb5452d937f6]] and Johannes Berglund among the producers, with more direct political and sexual themes than the 2009 debut. "Wanna Sip" (January 23, 2018) and "IDK About You" (March 1, 2018) followed.

years.cap: Fever Ray at Roskilde Festival, Denmark, July 2018
years.h: The Plunge tour opens in Europe in February and reaches North America in May
years.p: More European dates ran from June through November. Dreijer's team won Producer of the Year at the 2018 Swedish Grammis.
years.xp: Wikipedia says Plunge was also nominated for IMPALA's Best European Independent Album.

years.big: "Music works for me as a totally open space."
years.src: NPR: Fever Ray · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: From 2019, Dreijer goes by they/them in English and hen in Swedish
years.p: Dreijer told NPR in 2023 that making music doesn't force them to think about gender much, unlike real life.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes Dreijer calling themself "definitely a queer person" and "very gender-fluid." NPR has them going on: in real life, "you have to think about it all the time."

years.h: Björk and Fever Ray swap remixes on Country Creatures
years.p: Each remixes a track from the other's 2017 album (Plunge and Björk's Utopia), and The Knife add a third remix even though they split in 2014.
years.xp: Wikipedia says the three remixes came out digitally September 6, 2019 and on a One Little Indian 12-inch on November 1.

eras.title: Love, with a long guest list
eras.text: Fever Ray's third album is about love, with Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross among the producers. Pitchfork puts it at No. 8 for 2023.

years.src: NPR: Fever Ray · Wikipedia: Radical Romantics
years.h: "What They Call Us" arrives first, with Olof Dreijer on synths
years.p: It comes in October 2022. "Carbon Dioxide," produced with Vessel, follows in November.

years.src: PAPER: Fever Ray and Martin Falck Kandy
years.h: Martin Falck directs the "Kandy" video
years.p: The third single's video arrives ahead of the March 10 album, and Falck shares behind-the-scenes photos with PAPER.

years.cap: Fever Ray at Terminal 5, New York, May 2023
years.src: Album of the Year · Wikipedia: Radical Romantics · NPR: Fever Ray
years.h: Pitchfork scores Radical Romantics 8.4 and puts it No. 8 for 2023
years.p: Rabid and Mute released it on March 10. Dreijer co-produced with Olof Dreijer, Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, Vessel, Nídia and others.
years.xp:
Wikipedia and Album of the Year both report Pitchfork's score as 8.4 (84), with Anna Gaca writing that the record renders "the search for love as something both sensual and alien." Uncut gave it 8.7. Not everyone bit: Slant asked where an artist this singular goes from here, and The Arts Desk said it "sounds exactly like a Fever Ray album." It ranked 28th in The Wire's year-end poll.

NPR reads the record as love treated as ongoing work, not a destination. Dreijer told NPR that "radical acceptance" of what you need to feel safe and loved brings stillness and also sadness. Other producers include Pär Grindvik, Peder Mannerfelt and Aasthma, with Johannes Berglund on vocal production.

years.h: The Year of the Radical Romantics puts the tour on record
years.p: Out July 25, a live album that pairs tracks from Radical Romantics and Plunge with reworked older songs from the There's No Place I'd Rather Be Tour.
